title: Merton, again
tomorrow: God asks Adam a question in a garden. what is it, and why ask?

segments.voice: Yesterday, John of the Cross and the dark night: the night taught. Today, someone who took off a mask in the daylight.

Every app wants a profile: the best photo, a clever bio, the version of you that gets the likes. A monk in Kentucky had a name for that version. He called it the false self, a mask we build for the world and then forget we're wearing. Here's the strange part. To find the face underneath, he took a new name, put on the same robe as every other monk in the house, and kept the same daily schedule as all of them. Then he wrote that for him, being a saint means being himself. A new name and a uniform, to become yourself? That sounds backwards.
screen: `THE PROFILE VERSION OF YOU.` → `THE FALSE SELF, A MASK.` → `A NEW NAME AND A UNIFORM?`

segments.voice: He's Thomas Merton, a writer who became a Trappist monk at the Abbey of Gethsemani, called Father Louis inside the walls. The puzzle solves like this. The false self, he wrote, is the one we assemble out of what others see: the highlight reel, the reputation, the image we polish and defend. It feels solid, but it's a costume. The true self is the person God sees and loves, hidden under all that, sometimes unknown even to us. So the robe and the new name weren't a disguise. They were a way of taking the costume off: no brand, nothing to perform. He used a tree to explain it. A tree, he said, gives glory to God by being a tree, not by trying to be something else. Holiness, in his telling, isn't becoming a copy of some other saint. It's becoming the one person God had in mind. Underneath sits a line from Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims: "to the image of God he created him." Something to tell a friend tonight: Merton's own mask-dropping moment didn't happen in a chapel. It happened on a busy street corner in Louisville, where he suddenly saw the strangers around him shining, and knew he loved them.
screen: `THE FALSE SELF: A COSTUME.` · `THE TRUE SELF: THE ONE GOD SEES.` · `A TREE, BEING A TREE.` · `A STREET CORNER IN LOUISVILLE.` · then, large: `TRUE SELF.`

segments.voice: Sit the way you sit when nobody's watching: not posed, not slumped for show. Open your hands on your knees with nothing in them, no phone and no role. For the sit, just be the person who is here, and if you pray, let God look at that one, no mask.
Merton. Thomas Merton, a Trappist monk and writer who said holiness means becoming your true self, the one God sees.
Pocket this one: true self, the face under the costume, the one God already sees. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: at a family party your cousin keeps changing how she talks depending on who's in the room, and she's exhausted. what would Merton point her toward?
options: the self under the roles, the one God sees, who doesn't have to perform.
a better mask: pick one version of herself and keep it everywhere.
leaving parties for good, since holiness means hiding from people.
fork.reveal: Merton's way out of the false self wasn't hiding: his own big moment was loving strangers on a busy Louisville street.

chat.says: Val says copy the highlight reel of the girl who got the big offer. ok but would that work?
options: Show your own game, not hers. Merton would say the real you is the one worth seeing.
Yes. Saints copy saints, so copying the best player is basically the holy move.
Skip the reel. Merton says wanting to be seen at all is just the false self.
chat.meaning: Merton's false self is the polished image; the true self is the one God sees. A tree gives glory by being a tree, not a copy.
